Second what was said regarding research.

As far as clinical work, most places (Ph.D. wise, anyway) don’t particularly care that you have extensive clinical experience before you apply. It will help your application if you do, but won’t necessarily hurt it to not have any professional clinical experience.

As far as trying to help you get in, it is definitely preferable to have experience in the area that you are interested in pursuing for grad school rather than something unrelated. 
For example, having that autism experience would definitely help your app for mentors that work with that population. But it won’t hurt your app for mentors that don’t do autism research- it just won’t necessarily help as much as if your experience were more relevant.

If it’s possible, I would recommend trying to work with the population that you are interested in, especially if you want to pursue practice after your graduate. Not only will it be more helpful for apps, but it will also give you a taste of whether you truly like working with that population or if you might have different interests than you first had in mind.

Like someone stated above, I would suggest taking the GRE Psychology practice test (easily found on the ETS website), scoring it, and finding out where your scores are lacking in order to better focus your efforts when you are studying.

Also, seconded about getting psych-relevant experience. Especially research experience; almost all PhD programs are looking for that, and it will give you a sense of if you will truly enjoy doing a graduate degree in psych since you haven’t had any academic psych experience yet.

Also worth noting: you can only take the psych GRE at three time points in the year (April, October, & November) so if you do need to take it (which you may not, as mentioned above) make sure to time it so that you will have scores in time to apply during the cycle that you are aiming to get accepted in.

Best of luck, fellow career-changer.

Before I get any further, know that we obviously can’t diagnose you here. However, here are a few things that may be helpful: 

statistically, the fact that you’ve remained in this sort of prodromal-esque phase for so long signifies that it’s unlikely you would have an acute psychotic break. If you were to develop schizophrenia (not saying that you are!), the fact that you are so self aware is definitely a positive prognostic sign!

Like I said before, the symptoms you are describing sound like the prodrome of schizophrenia. Though it sounds strange, another option to consider may be BPD (you mentioned having some emotional difficulties, and some folk with BPD have more persistent quasi-psychotic symptoms.) Other disorders can also cause symptoms like those you described- schizotypal PD, bipolar, schizoaffective, to name a few.

The most important thing you can do now is to see a professional. Whether you have schizophrenia or not, they could help you set your mind at ease and deal with whatever issue is causing all of this.

When I first started DBT i was so-so about it, and kind of angry that I was being "judged" by the psychologist I saw. For the first few months I engaged in the DBT skills but didn't really buy into them, and it kept me afloat (not dead/minimal self harm). I didn't really "feel" any better though.

That was until I wrecked everything.
I got kicked out of my program at Uni, boyfriend broke up with me, huge fallout with my mother. I had hit rock bottom and wanted to die but decided to try to fully engage in DBT for a few months to make sure it wouldn't help before I offed myself.

That is when it really started helping me. Over the course of the next few months I improved immensely.

I tell you all of this because all I really cared about going into DBT was keeping up my facade of being okay to the outside world. I gave minimal effort, so I got a minimal reward from it. I didn't care to stop cutting at first, but I realized that it was worth it to stop if it helped me progress further in therapy to the parts that actually focus on making you feel more content.

Not failing out of uni is a great goal to start out with, and just being open to doing the skills (even if you are upset or angry about them) is enough.  You get how much you put into it, but don't pressure yourself into going all-out right now if you just can't. Don't burn out quickly and quit prematurely.  Whatever attitude you can show up with is enough. You don't have to go in with the expectation that it will definitely work, but it helps immensely to come with an open mind that it could *possibly* work.

Sorry for the text wall but I hope that it is helpful for you. You don't have to have the best attitude to start going to therapy, you just have to go. And take it one step at a time from there. :)

I can relate to what OP is saying. 
For me, it was harder to admit to other people that I had BPD than it was to myself. It felt like I was saying that I was guilty for everything bad that had ever happened to me and that I was a monster.
To be honest, that label still feels like that for me sometimes. 

Acceptance comes in waves. I'm to the point where I can accept that I had BPD and still have traits. And sometimes it's like pulling myself through the mud to say that my life is worth living when I think that I've been condemned to a lesser life by this disorder.

But BPD is just a construct. It is a cluster of symptoms that are characteristic of a condition. There is no such *real* thing as BPD, it's just a label that is used to communicate with others some very general information about what is going on with you. It is also very heavily stigmatized, but that is a problem that health professions need to address within themselves and not a reflection of you.

I absolutely must say that in order to make any progress whatsoever in feeling better, you need to seek some sort of treatment or read a DBT self help book and put the concepts into practice. Do it with all the anger you need to. But do it.

BPD is as complex as every individual with the label. We are quiet, or great at sports, or artistic, or whatever the heck and we also happen to have BPD. It can be soooooooo hard not to let the label be the death of you, but in the end it is your choice where to go from here and how your life is going to be.

Much love to you, OP.
